rows.description: A young child can learn to breathe slowly by blowing bubbles, smelling a flower and blowing out a candle. Practised when calm, this gives the child a tool that is easier to reach when upset.
A student about to present slows the exhale, drops the shoulders and pauses before the first sentence. The steadier breath calms the voice and thinking, and does not need anyone to notice it.
A student sees a rumour about a teacher spread through school until everyone treats it as fact; every repetition makes it feel more believable and harder to question.
An adult sees one dramatic news story about a rare event push the whole locality into over-caution while common everyday risks are ignored.
A teenager learns to criticise the act or plan rather than the person, and to accept feedback without collapsing or attacking. "That part is unclear" is more usable than "You are useless".

rows.subtype: Taking criticism without shrinking or bristling [Regulating]
rows.description: A young adult listens to feedback, asks clarifying questions and separates useful points from unfair ones. Immediate defence or total self-blame both make learning harder.

rows.subtype: Scolding and reprimanding as a supervisor [Regulating]
rows.description: A young supervisor reprimands by describing the behaviour and its impact, keeping voice calm and giving a path to improve. Sarcasm, humiliation or repeated scolding harms the relationship and can amount to bullying.
A child who commands peers may be leading, anxious, or copying adult tone. Adults can coach the child to swap commands for invitations, such as how about we.
A teenager weighs recommendations from friends and influencers about trends, products and risks. Advice that carries pressure to do something unsafe or secret is a reason to consult a trusted adult.

rows.subtype: Rituals to keep bad things away [Actor]
rows.description: A child repeats handwashing, touching or checking, or must say certain words to prevent harm. It feels unavoidable, and scolding makes it worse; a doctor or child psychologist can guide the family.
A teenager may have upsetting thoughts they hate and fear meaning something about them. Such thoughts are common and do not show who a person is; shame keeps them secret, and professional help works.
A young adult spends hours checking or arranging things, arrives late and hides it from friends. Compulsions relieve fear briefly and then demand more, and seeking a qualified clinician is wise.
A city child on a holiday sees animals, fields and a slower rhythm and is thrilled by mud and mangoes. It is easy to romanticise; the child may learn later of hard work behind such simplicity.
A villager sees urban youth as selfish, disconnected from family and soil. This is partly true of some and unfair to many; both sides carry stereotypes worth unlearning.
